result: Two-photon calcium imaging effectively detects neuronal activity during artificial whisking with robust and reproducible whisker movements across different texture coarseness.
evaluation: Claims C21-C26 demonstrate that calcium imaging reliably detects action potentials (82-91% detection rate for single spikes, essentially all spike trains), calcium transients are locked to whisking, whisker movements are consistent across trials, and differences in whisker curvature and stick-slip events are observed between textures. The combined electrophysiological validation and kinematic measurements provide strong technical validation.

result: Layer 2-3 neurons within barrel boundaries differentially respond to specific texture coarseness, with most neurons showing preferential responses to one texture rather than monotonic responses across coarseness.
evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C27-C29, C33-C34 collectively demonstrate that 54.4±3.5% of neurons show texture preference, only a minority show monotonic responses, many prefer specific textures, and 90.6±3.2% show consistent preferred texture when measured by peak vs. area. The calcium imaging data (Figures 3, 4) and electrophysiological validation provide converging evidence.

result: Texture coarseness selective neurons are almost exclusively confined to barrel boundaries, while septal neurons show minimal texture selectivity.
evaluation: Claims C30-C32, C39, C66 demonstrate through histological alignment with single-cell resolution that texture-selective neurons are within barrel boundaries, septal neurons are non-responsive or show low selectivity (S.I.<0.35), with only ~10% smaller calcium transients in septa. The biocytin electroporation method (Figure 2) provides rigorous anatomical validation.

result: Neurons with similar texture coarseness preference are spatially clustered in layer 2-3 of the barrel cortex.
evaluation: Claims C5, C36-C37 show spatial clustering with 49.0±3.9% probability of same-preference nearest neighbors vs. 23.6±3.4% expected by chance (p<0.01). Both closest neighbor analysis and Monte Carlo analysis (Figure 5) demonstrate significant clustering beyond random distribution for cells with S.I.≥0.35 and all neurons.

result: Texture coarseness preference is spatially organized along the rostro-medial to caudo-lateral diagonal of the barrel, with coarser textures preferentially represented at barrel perimeters.
evaluation: Claims C40-C41, C64 demonstrate diagonal organization (p<0.01, 4-way ANOVA) with P120 rostro-medial and P1000 caudo-lateral, and coarser textures (P120/P320) at significantly larger radial distances than finer textures (P600/P1000) (p<0.01). The normalized barrel analysis across 12 experiments (Figure 6C) provides robust spatial mapping evidence.

result: Texture coarseness preference shows vertical columnar organization across the depth of layer 2-3.
evaluation: Claims C6, C42-C43 demonstrate columnar organization with 3.5-fold higher probability of same texture preference across all electrode contacts than expected by chance for selective cells (S.I.>0.34) and 2.2-fold for all cells. Multi-contact electrode recordings (Figure 7) across 250-500 μm depth show neurons retain texture preference vertically.

result: Passive replay of texture-like vibrations reproduces the spatial clustering and diagonal organization observed during artificial whisking.
evaluation: Claims C44-C49 show that passive stimulation yields similar results: 84.1±13.4% responsive neurons, 52.7±8.12% selective (S.I.>0.35), spatial clustering (40.9±6.1% vs. 24.2±4.0% expected, p<0.01), and diagonal organization. This well-controlled paradigm (Figure 8-9) validates findings from artificial whisking and rules out experimental variability.

result: Electrophysiological recordings show lower percentage of non-responsive neurons (2±1.3%) compared to calcium imaging, likely due to larger number of repetitions.
evaluation: Claim C35 is supported by the electrophysiological data (Figure 4B) and provides a reasonable explanation for the difference. The inference about repetition number is plausible given the methodological differences described.

result: Layer 2-3 neurons perform high hierarchical processing of tactile information with texture coarseness embodied by distinct spatially-mapped neuronal subpopulations, representing a higher processing station than layer 4.
evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C70-C72 synthesize the experimental findings into a coherent interpretation. The differential responses, spatial clustering, and columnar organization (C3-C6, C36-C43) support this conclusion. The comparison to layer 4 rate coding is supported by cited literature, making this a well-justified interpretation of the data.

result: The barrel cortex exhibits a novel spatio-functional organization with texture-selective neuron clustering, contrasting with the 'salt and pepper' organization in rat visual and auditory cortices, representing the second functional map in S1 barrels.
evaluation: Claims C63, C65 are supported by the spatial clustering data (C36-C41) and appropriately contextualized with cited comparative studies (C60-C62). The conclusion that this is the second map (after angular direction) is justified by the current findings and cited previous work (C18-C19).

result: A coding scheme based on coarseness-selective neurons can increase reliability of texture discrimination by comparing activity across neurons with different tuning, potentially being less sensitive to animal state than population averaging schemes.
evaluation: Claims C57-C58 are theoretical interpretations marked as INFERENCE/SPECULATION. While the existence of coarseness-selective neurons is well-supported, the comparative advantages of this coding scheme over alternatives require direct experimental testing that was not performed in this study.

result: Texture coding is performed mostly by barrel neurons, with coarseness cluster formation potentially resulting from feedforward connectivity and local circuit mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C69, C73 are explicitly marked as requiring confirmation in awake animals (C69) and as hypotheses not investigated in this study (C73). While the barrel vs. septa differences are well-documented (C30-C32, C66-C68), the mechanistic claims and functional implications require additional experimental validation.

result: Artificial whisking kinematics closely simulate freely behaving rats, and texture-responding neurons have been detected in awake behaving mice.
evaluation: Claims C50-C51 are based on appropriate citations to recent studies (Bagdasarian et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2013) that provide external validation for the experimental approach and findings. These claims appropriately contextualize the current work.
